outcome: No result since 26 January 2024 changes the classification of pairs of n×n matrices under simultaneous conjugation; the two candidate papers found by searches both address distinct, related problems (a different equivalence relation, and a finite-field algorithmic variant), and the classical wild problem itself is a long-standing complexity benchmark rather than an active open conjecture with a research program aimed at resolving it.
summary: The Wikipedia bullet describes the classical 'wild problem': classifying pairs of n×n matrices under simultaneous conjugation (A,B) ↦ (S⁻¹AS, S⁻¹BS). This is not an open conjecture in the usual sense but a decades-old benchmark of representation-theoretic complexity, formalized by Yu. A. Drozd's tame/wild dichotomy: a classification problem is 'wild' precisely when it contains (is at least as hard as) this matrix-pair problem, which is considered intractable/'hopeless' to classify explicitly because it is known to encode the representation theory of arbitrary finitely generated algebras. Nothing in the mathematical literature treats this as a problem awaiting resolution — its content (that no tractable classification exists) was established well before 2024, so there is no pending resolution for a 2024-2026 result to deliver. Triage found two 2024 papers: arXiv:2408.04244 ('Polynomial similarity of pairs of matrices', published in Linear Algebra and its Applications vol. 708, 2025) proves that classification under a different, weaker equivalence relation ('polynomial similarity', involving polynomial coordinate changes plus similarity, restricted to commuting nilpotent pairs) is itself wild by reduction to the classical problem — this is a related problem (a different equivalence relation), not a case of the stated problem, and it does not change the classical statement. arXiv:2409.12457 ('Canonical forms for matrix tuples in polynomial time', FOCS 2024) gives polynomial-time algorithms for computing canonical forms of matrix tuples over finite fields under conjugation and left-right actions — this is an algorithmic/computational question about a specific setting (finite fields, isomorphism/canonical-form testing) that coexists with wildness (wildness is about the impossibility of a tame parametrized classification, not about computational infeasibility of canonical-form algorithms) and is a related but distinct problem, not a resolution or partial resolution of the stated classification problem. I opened both papers directly (via WebFetch) rather than relying on titles/snippets, confirming triage's reading in both cases. I also checked the current Wikipedia 'Wild problem' article, which contains no update reflecting any 2024-2026 development. No source anywhere mentions AI, machine learning, or automated theorem proving in connection with this problem or either paper. I agree with the triage verdict of 'none' and its scope classification of both found items as variants rather than cases.
competing_reading: One could argue arXiv:2409.12457's polynomial-time canonical-form algorithm for matrix tuples over finite fields is a 'case' of the stated problem restricted to finite fields — if so it would be `partial` progress with `ai_role` none. I reject this reading because the stated problem is about classification (a normal-form/parametrization question showing the parameter space structure, which wildness says is intractable in a technical representation-theoretic sense), whereas the FOCS paper is about the different question of algorithmically computing/testing canonical forms and isomorphism given specific matrix tuples over a finite field — a computational complexity question that is compatible with, and does not resolve or restrict, the classification-theoretic wildness statement (the paper itself does not claim to make progress on or resolve any case of the wildness classification). It also is not confined to n×n conjugation of pairs (it covers general tuples and multiple groups of actions), further indicating a different-but-related problem rather than a restriction of the exact stated one.
what_would_settle_it: A paper explicitly reducing part of the classical simultaneous-conjugation classification problem to a tame/tractable sub-case (e.g., a bounded-dimension case proven tame where previously open) would settle the ambiguity in favor of `partial`; absent that, the current reading (both found papers are related-but-distinct problems) stands.
